title: Checkpoint: Elections
objective: After this level you can explain how elections turn votes into power.
summary: The IPU's 1994 Declaration on free and fair elections lists this chapter's ideas: authority from the people, a secret and equal vote, fair campaigns and an honest, observed count.

cards.headline: In 1994, the Inter-Parliamentary Union wrote a checklist for fair elections.
cards.body: On 26 March 1994 in Paris, the Inter-Parliamentary Council unanimously adopted the IPU's Declaration on Criteria for Free and Fair Elections. Read it now and it looks like this chapter's table of contents.

items.label: Where power comes from
points: Authority only from the will of the people

items.label: How you vote
points: The right to vote in secret is absolute (Level 62)

items.label: The race and the count
points: An honest count, with party agents and observers (Level 68)

cards.headline: From a ballot to power
cards.body: Follow one vote through this chapter. It's cast in secret, turned into seats by a voting system and a district map, fought over in a campaign and counted in the open. What comes out is Level 3's authority: power people accept as legitimate. And Popper's point makes it complete: the ruled can dismiss their rulers without bloodshed, so next time the same vote can take that power away.

mascot.line: Ten levels, and you can follow a vote from the ballot box all the way to power.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: IPU, 1994: criteria for free and fair elections
Authority from the will of the people, at regular intervals
Secret, equal votes; fair campaigns; an honest count
Elections both grant power and take it back

questions.prompt: According to the IPU's 1994 Declaration, which voting right is absolute?

options.label: The right to vote in secret
The right to a recount on demand
options.rationale: Recounts are a UK counting rule, not the Declaration's absolute right.

options.label: The right to vote by ranking
options.rationale: The Declaration doesn't choose a voting system.

options.label: The right to vote in public
options.rationale: It's secrecy that the Declaration makes absolute.

questions.explanation: The Declaration says the right to vote in secret is absolute and shall not be restricted in any manner.

questions.prompt: Elections checkpoint: which list puts these in order, oldest first?

options.label: Victoria ballot → Gerry-mander → Digest poll → NZ MMP vote
options.rationale: The Gerry-mander (1812) is older than Victoria's ballot (1856).

options.label: Gerry-mander → Victoria ballot → Digest poll → NZ MMP vote
Gerry-mander → Digest poll → Victoria ballot → NZ MMP vote
options.rationale: Victoria's ballot (1856) came before the Digest poll (1936).

options.label: Digest poll → Gerry-mander → NZ MMP vote → Victoria ballot
options.rationale: The 1936 poll is the second-newest of these.

questions.explanation: The Gerry-mander (1812), Victoria's secret ballot (1856), the Literary Digest poll (1936), New Zealand's first MMP election (1996).

questions.prompt: Back to Level 63: under the Alternative Vote used for Australia's House of Representatives, what happens if nobody has a majority?

options.label: The candidate with the most first choices wins anyway
Seats are shared out by vote share
The last are eliminated and votes transferred
The election is held again a month later
options.rationale: The count continues with transferred votes instead.

questions.explanation: Under the Alternative Vote, the least successful candidates are eliminated and their votes transferred until someone has a majority.

questions.prompt: The IPU Declaration says every vote should carry equivalent weight. Which Level 64 practice most directly works against that?

options.label: Counting in front of candidates' agents
Packing and cracking district voters
Printing ballot papers by the government
options.rationale: That's the Victorian secret ballot, not a threat.

options.label: Ranking candidates by preference
options.rationale: Ranking is a voting method, not a way to skew districts.

questions.explanation: Packing and cracking leave a group with fewer seats than its votes suggest, so its votes weigh less.

questions.prompt: In 1988 Chile's Pinochet lost a referendum, and his regime collapsed soon after. Which Level 61 thinker's test of democracy does that peaceful removal echo?

options.label: Joseph Schumpeter's
options.rationale: Schumpeter stressed competing for votes; dismissal without bloodshed is Popper's test.

options.label: John Stuart Mill's
options.rationale: Mill argued about public voting, not dismissing rulers.

options.label: Maurice Duverger's
options.rationale: Duverger studied voting systems and party numbers.

options.label: Karl Popper's

questions.explanation: Popper's test is whether the ruled can dismiss their rulers without bloodshed.
